questions.q: What is the actual gap between "vm-catalog01 exists" and "the catalog app is running on vm-catalog01"?
options: There is no gap -- creating the VM automatically runs the app
The runtime the app needs must be installed, the application code copied over, and the app started as a managed service -- none of which `az vm create` does
The gap is only closed by rebooting the VM
The gap is closed automatically once a public IP is assigned
questions.explain: A VM existing and a VM running the catalog app are two different states. Getting from one to the other means installing the runtime, deploying the code, and starting it as a service.

questions.q: Why does the NSG only get one new rule (port 80, or 443 for TLS) rather than opening a wider range of ports?
options: Azure NSGs can only ever have exactly two rules
Opening exactly the traffic the app needs, and nothing more, mirrors what a correctly configured on-prem firewall would already do -- opening more "to be safe" isn't actually safe
Port 80 is the only port Azure VMs support
Wider port ranges cost extra in Azure
questions.explain: The point is opening exactly the path the app needs. A wider-open NSG isn't a safety margin, it's unnecessary exposure.

questions.q: Why doesn't a VM showing "Running" in `az vm list` prove the migration is working?
options: It does prove it -- no further check is needed
"Running" only describes the VM's power state, not whether the application inside it is actually serving requests correctly
"Running" status is unreliable and often wrong
VM status only updates once per day
questions.explain: "Running" is a VM power state. Whether the catalog app itself is answering requests needs a real check, like `curl -I` returning a 200 OK and the pages loading correctly in a browser.

options: That the product images have been migrated correctly
That the web server on the VM is answering HTTP requests, by checking the response headers
That the VM's disk has enough free space
That the NSG has no rules configured
questions.explain: `curl -I` requests just the HTTP headers -- a fast way to confirm the web server actually responds, before doing a deeper check like loading pages in a browser.

questions.q: Which of these is consistent with this lesson's "lift-and-shift, not a redesign" approach?
options: Adding a load balancer and auto-scaling group during this migration
Running the app on one VM, reachable by its public IP, with the only functional code change being the Lesson 4 image URL update
Rewriting the catalog app as a set of microservices
Building a full CI/CD pipeline before the app is even running once
questions.explain: This lesson deliberately keeps the setup close to the on-prem original -- one VM, the same running shape, with the image URL change being the only functional change required.
